top_level_objectives: Apply VSEPR theory to predict electron-domain geometries.
Explain how lone pairs influence molecular shape and bond angles.
Compare theoretical repulsion models with actual molecular structures.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the core principle that electron domains minimize repulsion.
key_visuals: Floating electron cloud balloons around a central point
student_actions: Drag and drop two, three, or four balloon-like electron clouds around a center point and observe them snap into symmetric arrangements.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore the five parent geometries derived from VSEPR.
key_visuals: A dynamic selector panel for 2 through 6 electron domains
student_actions: Select different domain counts to visualize linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral parent shapes.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how replacing bonding pairs with lone pairs alters geometry.
key_visuals: Methane tetrahedral structure transforming into ammonia and water
student_actions: Toggle between bonding pairs and lone pairs on the central atom and observe the resulting change in molecular shape name and bond angle.

scenes.brief_purpose: Map theoretical geometries to experimental chemical data.
key_visuals: 3D molecular models of CH4, NH3, and H2O
student_actions: Interact with labels on real molecules to see how the observed bond angles deviate from the idealized predictions due to lone-pair repulsion.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore non-octet configurations like PF5 and SF6.
student_actions: Rotate the SF6 model to identify equatorial vs. axial positions and predict where lone pairs would occupy space first.

scenes.brief_purpose: Apply the theory to an unknown or chosen molecule.
key_visuals: A blank workbench with a central atom and various bonding components
student_actions: Construct a molecule from a provided Lewis structure and verify if the final 3D geometry matches their prediction.
